html:
After the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, most Bukharan Jews left Central Asia within about a decade, for Israel and the United States, ending many centuries of Jewish life in cities like Bukhara and Samarkand.

Bukharan Jews are a Persian-speaking Jewish community named after the Emirate of Bukhara, one of the Uzbek khanates. They trace their roots to the Jews of ancient Persia, and they spoke Bukhori, a Jewish form of Tajik Persian. Under the emirs they lived in their own quarter, paid a special tax and had to dress apart; many were dyers and cloth merchants. Under Soviet rule synagogues were closed, but families kept their customs.

Some left for Israel in the 1970s, and with the Soviet collapse, the civil war in Tajikistan and fear of rising nationalism, the trickle became an exodus. Only small numbers remain. Large communities grew in Israel and in Queens, New York, around Forest Hills and Rego Park. In the same years the descendants of the deported Volga Germans left Central Asia for Germany.
sum: After the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, most Bukharan Jews left Central Asia within about a decade, for Israel and the United States, ending many centuries of Jewish life in cities like Bukhara and Samarkand.
